lessons.title: bigger, biggest — comparison
lessons.summary: Add -er to compare two things and am -sten for the winner — then learn the five irregulars and stop mixing up als and wie.
lessons.rule:
An adjective is a describing word: big, old, cheap. When you hold two things next to each other you need a stronger version of it — bigger, older, cheaper. That stronger version has a name: the comparative. And when one thing beats everything else you need the top version — biggest, oldest — called the superlative. German builds both almost exactly the way English does with short words, so this lesson is mostly good news.

Comparing two things: add -er. klein → kleiner, schnell → schneller, billig → billiger. German does this to every adjective, no matter how long it is. English gives up on long words and switches to more (more interesting), and Turkish puts daha in front. German never does either. It is interessanter, wichtiger, bequemer — never mehr interessant.

The winner: am plus -sten. am kleinsten, am schnellsten, am billigsten. Two small adjustments. If the adjective ends in d, t, s, z or ß, an extra e slides in so your mouth can manage it: alt → am ältesten, kurz → am kürzesten. And many short one-syllable adjectives grow an Umlaut — the two dots — as soon as they are compared: alt → älter, jung → jünger, lang → länger, warm → wärmer. There is no rule for which ones do this. It is a small memorised group, and the second table below is most of it.

Now the part people get wrong for years: wie or als? If the two things are equal, use the pair so … wie: Ich bin so groß wie du. If one is more than the other, use als: Ich bin größer als du. The test is mechanical — the moment there is an -er form in the sentence, the next little word is als. You will hear people in Berlin say größer wie du; it is still marked wrong in writing and in every exam, so do not copy it.

One more thing you will see everywhere. Next to am besten there is a second superlative that stands directly in front of a noun and takes an ending: der beste Kaffee, die größte Stadt, mein bester Freund. Same meaning, different position. Use am …sten after a verb, and der/die/das …ste in front of a noun.

tables.title: Short adjectives that grow two dots
The five irregulars you simply memorise

examples.note: groß takes the two dots and the -er, and als is the word for than.

examples.de: Ich bin so alt wie mein Bruder.
examples.en: I am the same age as my brother.
examples.note: Equal, so no -er at all — just the plain adjective inside so … wie.

examples.de: Der Zug ist nicht so teuer wie das Flugzeug.
examples.en: The train is not as expensive as the plane.
examples.note: nicht so … wie is how you say less than something, without changing the adjective.

examples.de: Ich trinke gern Tee, aber lieber Kaffee.
examples.en: I like tea, but I prefer coffee.
examples.note: lieber is the comparative of gern. It has nothing to do with the word lieb.
gut is fully irregular: gut, besser, am besten. There is no gutsten.

examples.de: Heute ist es kälter als gestern.
examples.en: Today it is colder than yesterday.
examples.note: Everyday weather talk — kalt gets its umlaut, and als follows the -er form.

mistakes.why: wie is only for things that are equal. Once you have an -er form, the sentence needs als.
German never builds a comparative with mehr, however long the adjective is. It is always the -er ending.

mistakes.wrong: Ich bin so groß als du.
mistakes.right: Ich bin so groß wie du.
mistakes.why: The mirror mistake. so belongs with wie, always — the two words come as a pair.

mistakes.wrong: Meine Schwester ist alter als ich.
mistakes.right: Meine Schwester ist älter als ich.
mistakes.why: Short adjectives like alt, jung, lang, warm and kalt take the two dots. Without them, alter is a different word that means an old thing, not older.

drills.question: Berlin ist ___ als Hamburg.
drills.explain: Two cities are being held against each other, so the -er form — and the als sitting there confirms it.

drills.question: Ich bin so alt ___ du.
drills.explain: The adjective has no -er ending, which means the two people are equal, and equality always uses so … wie.

drills.question: Kaffee trinke ich ___ als Tee.
drills.explain: gern is one of the five irregulars — it does not take -er, it turns into the separate word lieber.

drills.question: Welches Handy ist ___?
drills.explain: After a verb the top form is am plus -sten, and billig needs no extra vowel.

drills.question: Der Winter in Berlin ist ___ als in Istanbul. (kalt)
drills.explain: kalt is a short adjective, so it grows the two dots before taking the -er.

drills.question: Mein Deutsch wird jeden Tag ___. (gut)
drills.explain: gut never takes an -er ending; its comparative is a completely different word.

drills.answer: Der Zug ist schneller als das Auto
drills.explain: The verb keeps position two, the comparative follows it, and als introduces the thing being beaten.
am liebsten is the top form of gern and travels as one two-word block right after the verb.

lessons.title: sich freuen, sich waschen — reflexive verbs
lessons.summary: Some German verbs need a small extra word pointing back at the doer — and the ones English leaves unmarked are exactly the ones you will forget.
lessons.rule:
Usually an action goes out from you and lands on something else: Ich wasche das Auto. Sometimes it loops back and lands on you: Ich wasche mich. — I wash myself. That little word pointing back at the doer is called a reflexive pronoun, and a verb that needs one is a reflexive verb. Turkish handles this inside the verb itself (yıkanmak); German uses a separate word that you must remember to say out loud.

In a dictionary these verbs are listed with sich stuck to the front — sich waschen, sich freuen. Treat that sich the way you treat der, die and das on a noun: it is part of the word, learn them together. In a real sentence the sich changes to match whoever is doing it, and it sits right after the conjugated verb: Ich freue mich. Heute freue ich mich. Freust du dich? Only ich and du have two different shapes to worry about; everybody else uses sich, uns or euch for both jobs.

Which shape — mich or mir? Two of German's grammar jobs are involved. The accusative is the thing the action lands on directly. The dative is the person the action is done for or to. So: Ich wasche mich. — nothing else is being washed, only me, so the accusative mich. But Ich wasche mir die Hände. — now die Hände is the thing being washed, so I step back into the dative mir, meaning for myself. The rule in practice: if a second thing appears after the pronoun, switch to the dative. Same with Ich putze mir die Zähne. and Ich ziehe mir eine Jacke an.

The real trap is not the endings. It is the verbs that carry a pronoun in German while English says nothing at all, so you will simply leave it out. Learn these as fixed phrases:

  • sich freuen — to be glad, to look forward to
  • sich erinnern an — to remember
  • sich beeilen — to hurry
  • sich entschuldigen — to apologise
  • sich vorstellen — to introduce yourself
  • sich setzen — to sit down
  • sich fühlen — to feel
  • sich interessieren für — to be interested in

Two practical notes. sich vorstellen means two different things depending on the shape: Ich stelle mich vor is I introduce myself, while Ich stelle mir das vor is I imagine that. And you will hear the polite version constantly in Germany — Setzen Sie sich, bitte. at the doctor, Beeilen Sie sich! on a platform. With Sie the pronoun is always sich, with a small s.

tables.title: When does mich become mir?
rows: Nothing else is being washed — only me.
die Hände is the thing washed, so mir just says whose.
Getting dressed, no second thing named.
Ich ziehe mir eine Jacke an.
eine Jacke is the thing, mir says for whom.

tables.title: Reflexive in German, invisible in English

examples.de: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
examples.en: I am looking forward to the weekend.
examples.note: freuen cannot stand alone. The mich is not decoration — without it the sentence is broken.

examples.de: Wir müssen uns beeilen, der Bus kommt.
examples.en: We have to hurry, the bus is coming.
examples.note: With a modal verb the pronoun stays near the front and beeilen goes to the very end.
die Hände is what gets washed, so the pronoun steps back into the dative mir.
English uses no extra word here at all. German needs dich, and it comes right after the subject.

examples.de: Darf ich mich vorstellen? Ich heiße Emre.
examples.en: May I introduce myself? My name is Emre.
examples.note: Say this at every first meeting. mich sits after ich, and the separable vorstellen waits at the end.
You will hear this at the doctor and at the Amt. With Sie the pronoun is always sich.

mistakes.right: Ich freue mich auf das Wochenende.
mistakes.why: English has no extra word here, so this is the easiest one in the world to drop. freuen does not exist without its pronoun.

mistakes.wrong: Er freut mich über das Geschenk.
mistakes.right: Er freut sich über das Geschenk.
mistakes.why: The pronoun must copy the doer. People learn ich freue mich as one chunk and then reuse mich for everybody — but er takes sich.
As soon as a second thing (die Hände) is what actually gets washed, the pronoun switches from accusative to dative.

mistakes.right: Ich erinnere mich an den Termin.
mistakes.why: sich erinnern needs both the pronoun and an. In German you do not remember a thing, you remind yourself of it.

drills.question: Ich freue ___ auf das Wochenende.
drills.explain: The doer is ich and nothing else is named after the pronoun, so the accusative shape.

drills.question: Er freut ___ über das Geschenk.
drills.explain: The pronoun always matches the doer, and everything except ich and du uses sich or uns or euch.

drills.question: Ich wasche ___ die Hände.
drills.explain: die Hände is already the thing being washed, so the person steps back into the dative.

drills.question: ___ Sie sich bitte!
drills.explain: The polite form uses the full -en verb with Sie, and its pronoun is sich.

drills.question: Wir treffen ___ um acht Uhr. (sich treffen)
drills.explain: wir takes uns, and the plural forms are identical in both cases so there is nothing to decide.

drills.question: Ich erinnere ___ nicht an seinen Namen. (sich erinnern)
drills.explain: erinnern is reflexive in German even though remember is not in English, and no second thing follows the pronoun.
The pronoun follows the conjugated verb muss, while the reflexive verb itself is parked at the end.
In a question word question the verb comes second and the subject Sie next, so sich lands just behind the subject.

lessons.title: Telling someone what to do
lessons.summary: Three command forms for three kinds of you — and the polite one is what you will actually hear on the train, at the doctor and at the Amt.
lessons.rule:
An imperative is the form you use to tell or ask somebody to do something: Come in. Wait here. Sign there. German has three of them, because German has three words for you: du for one person you know, ihr for several people you know, and Sie for strangers, officials and anyone you have not been invited to call du.

The du command. Take the ordinary du form and chop off the -st: du gehst → Geh!, du kommst → Komm!, du machst → Mach!. And leave the word du out — the command carries no pronoun. Two details. If the stem ends in t or d, keep an -e so it is sayable: Warte!, Arbeite!. And if the du form changes its vowel from e to i, the command keeps that change: du nimmst → Nimm!, du gibst → Gib!, du sprichst → Sprich!, du liest → Lies!. But if the change was a to ä, the command throws the dots away again: du fährst → Fahr!, du schläfst → Schlaf!

The ihr command is the easy one: it is exactly the normal ihr form with the pronoun removed. Geht! Kommt! Wartet! Nehmt! The Sie command is also simple, and it is the only one that keeps its pronoun: the full -en verb, then Sie. Gehen Sie! Kommen Sie! Warten Sie! It looks identical to a statement with the words flipped, and that is all it is.

sein is the one genuinely irregular verb here: Sei ruhig!, Seid ruhig!, Seien Sie ruhig! — never Sind Sie. And a separable verb splits as usual, with its little front piece dropping to the end of the sentence: Steh bitte auf!, Macht die Tür zu!, Steigen Sie bitte ein!

One social point that matters more than the grammar. A bare command sounds sharp in German, so bitte goes in almost every one: Komm bitte um acht., Warten Sie bitte einen Moment. You will meet the Sie form constantly — Nehmen Sie bitte Platz. at the doctor, Steigen Sie bitte ein. on a platform, Füllen Sie das Formular aus. at the Amt. On written signs German often skips the imperative entirely and uses the plain dictionary form instead: Bitte nicht rauchen., Tür schließen., Drücken, Ziehen. Same meaning, no ending to worry about.

tables.title: What happens to the vowel
rows: the e to i change stays
the e to i change stays
the e to ie change stays

tables.title: Where you will actually meet it

examples.note: du form: the -st of du kommst is gone and the word du is not said.

examples.de: Nimm den Bus, das ist schneller.
examples.en: Take the bus, it is faster.
examples.note: nehmen keeps its e to i change in the command, so it is Nimm and never Nehm.
ihr form: exactly the everyday ihr verb with the pronoun taken away.

examples.de: Gehen Sie geradeaus und dann links.
examples.en: Go straight ahead and then left.
examples.note: The polite form keeps Sie. Ask for directions and this is what comes back at you.
sein is the one truly irregular command. Seien Sie, never Sind Sie.
A separable verb splits: mach at the front, and the little zu at the very end.

mistakes.why: The -st ending has to come off. Leave it on and you have just made an ordinary statement or half a question.
The du command never carries its pronoun. Only the polite Sie form keeps one.
If the du form swaps e for i (du nimmst, du gibst, du sprichst), the command keeps that vowel — though a to ä verbs lose their dots: du fährst gives Fahr!
The polite command is not the du form plus Sie. It is the full -en verb with Sie behind it, like a statement turned around.

drills.question: ___ bitte um acht! (to a friend)
drills.explain: The du command is the du form with the -st cut off and no pronoun.

drills.question: ___ Sie bitte einen Moment!
drills.explain: The polite command uses the full -en verb, and Sie stays right behind it.

drills.question: ___ den Bus, das ist schneller. (to a friend)
drills.explain: du nimmst already swaps e for i, and the command hangs on to that vowel.

drills.question: ___ bitte pünktlich! (to your boss)
drills.explain: sein is the only verb whose polite command is not just the dictionary form plus Sie.

drills.question: ___ langsam! (fahren, to a friend)
drills.explain: The a to ä swap is the one vowel change the command throws away again.

drills.question: ___ hier, Kinder! (warten, to several people)
drills.explain: The ihr command is simply the normal ihr form with the pronoun deleted.

drills.answer: Machen Sie bitte die Tür zu
drills.explain: Polite verb first, then Sie, and the separable piece zu is pushed to the very end.
The du command opens the sentence and the separable auf still has to wait at the end.
